row.basis: straight way to an inhabited city
row.note: After wilderness wandering, God leads the travellers by a straight way to a city where they can dwell; it gives the road the arrived-at end that the commentary says distinguishes sirat from disappearance.

row.basis: wanderers without a city
row.note: The travellers wander in a desert route and find no inhabited city, a concrete itinerary whose missing destination illuminates the commentary's person who goes away with no known arrival.

row.basis: highway where travellers do not err
row.note: Isaiah's holy highway is specifically a way on which even wayfarers do not go astray, closely joining a directed road to the commentary's contrast between sirat and dalal.

row.basis: straight path without stumbling
row.note: In the return-from-exile procession God leads people beside water on a straight path where they will not stumble; its physical homeward route gives a destination to divinely guided movement.

row.basis: guard on the way, brought to a place
row.note: The angel is sent ahead both to guard Israel on the way and to bring it to the prepared place, the same two-part image of guidance and arrival developed for the sirat.

row.basis: make a straight highway for God
row.note: The wilderness proclamation makes a straight highway for God's coming; it supplies the road-and-arrival imagery behind a straight way without reducing the Qur'anic prayer to a lexical match.

row.basis: Isaiah's straight paths applied to John's mission
row.note: Luke reuses the wilderness voice and straight paths for John the Baptist's preparation of the Lord's advent, a Christian framing of the same directed-road image.

row.basis: blind led on unknown paths
row.note: God leads blind people on ways they have not known and turns darkness to light before them; this is the salvific reversal of the commentary's sightless people unable to find the path.

row.basis: wicked way as darkness and unknown stumbling
row.note: The wicked walk in deep darkness and do not know over what they stumble, directly pairing loss of sight and loss of bearing as in the commentary's blind rush toward a road.

row.basis: path of righteousness is life
row.note: Proverbs makes the outcome explicit: the path of righteousness is life and its track has no death, sharpening the commentary's claim that the difference between two goings lies in where they lead.

row.basis: a seemingly right way ending in death
row.note: The proverb warns that a way which appears right can end in death, making destination rather than outward direction the test of a road.

row.basis: water vanishes from its place in heat
row.note: Job's seasonal streams are scorched and disappear from their place; this is a textual water-loss image beside the commentary's example of something consumed and lost in water.

row.basis: caravans leave their course and perish
row.note: The same wadi scene has caravan routes turn aside into waste and perish, bringing the commentary's linked images of vanishing water and travellers without a destination into one scene.

row.basis: wander in a pathless waste
row.note: God makes leaders wander in a trackless waste; its stated absence of a road concretizes dalal as a going whose direction cannot be found.

row.basis: grope in darkness and stagger
row.note: Those made to grope without light stagger like the drunk, supplying a close bodily counterpart to the commentary's blind people who cannot see a path.

row.basis: blind groping and stumbling
row.note: The people grope like the blind and stumble at midday as in twilight, a direct image of vision failing to orient movement.

row.basis: blind guides and a pit
row.note: Jesus' saying has a blind guide and blind follower both fall into a pit, making the commentary's sightless route-seeking and its well/pit image meet in one contrary destination.

row.basis: walking in darkness without knowing where one goes
row.note: Jesus says that the person walking in darkness does not know where he is going, an exact formulation of movement whose destination has vanished from knowledge.

row.basis: lost sheep led astray by shepherds
row.note: Jeremiah calls the people lost sheep whose shepherds led them astray across mountains; its failed guides give the commentary's dalal a communal and directional scene.

row.basis: seek the lost and bring back the strayed
row.note: God promises to seek the lost and bring back the strayed sheep, turning unknown disappearance into known recovery and return.

row.basis: straying sheep returned to their shepherd
row.note: The readers were straying like sheep but have returned to the shepherd, a concise Christian movement from lost wandering to a responsible destination.

row.basis: forsaking the straight way and going astray
row.note: The false teachers abandon the straight way and go astray, directly setting a right route against wandering in the terms the commentary contrasts.

row.basis: restricted way leading to life
row.note: The restricted way leads to life and is found by few; it makes the endpoint of a path, rather than mere motion, decisive.

row.basis: broad way leading to destruction
row.note: The broad road leads to destruction, furnishing the adverse route and end alongside Matthew's life-leading way.

row.basis: unknown destination and unknown way
row.note: Thomas explicitly links not knowing Jesus' destination with not knowing the way, the very relation between route and arrival made central in the commentary.

row.basis: Jesus as way to the Father
row.note: Jesus identifies himself as the way by which one comes to the Father; it is a Christian construal of a road whose point is arrival before God.

row.basis: Joseph cast into a wilderness pit
row.note: Reuben directs that Joseph be put into a pit in the wilderness rather than killed, giving the older narrative's concrete counterpart to Joseph's removal into the hidden bottom of a well.

row.basis: traders draw Joseph from the pit and take him to Egypt
row.note: Passing traders draw Joseph out and carry him toward Egypt, so the pit disappearance becomes a transit with an unforeseen destination, as the commentary emphasizes.

row.basis: Joseph sold into Egypt, yet God with him
row.note: Stephen's retelling retains the brothers' sale of Joseph but adds that God was with him, explicitly reading the apparent loss as a providentially accompanied passage.

row.basis: graves opened and people brought to their land
row.note: God opens graves, brings the dead up, and brings them into Israel's land; earth's enclosure is therefore a stage on a directed restoration, not their final disappearance.

row.basis: dwellers in dust awaken
row.note: The dead live and the dwellers in dust awake, a direct answer to the image of bodies hidden in earth and then newly created.

row.basis: sleepers in earth's dust awaken
row.note: Many sleeping in the dust of the earth awake for divergent final outcomes, closely matching burial in earth followed by new life and judgment.

row.basis: earth and Sheol return what was entrusted
row.note: The earth and Sheol give back what was entrusted to them; this treats apparent disappearance into the underworld as custody before eschatological return.

row.basis: earth and dust give up their sleepers
row.note: At judgment the earth gives up those asleep in it and dust those dwelling silently, an unusually close Jewish apocalyptic answer to people thought lost in earth.

row.basis: earth preserves and restores the dead
row.note: The earth receives the dead to preserve them and restores them as received, making burial a guarded holding rather than annihilation.

row.basis: all in tombs hear the summons
row.note: All who are in tombs hear the Son's voice; the verse denies that hidden burial places can make the dead unavailable to resurrection.

row.basis: emergence from tombs for judgment
row.note: Those in tombs come out for life or judgment, supplying both the new emergence and the accountable end that the commentary joins to earth-loss.

row.basis: sea, Death, and Hades give up their dead
row.note: The sea, Death, and Hades yield their dead for judgment, a precise final-assize counter-image to persons or things apparently lost in earth or water.

row.basis: raised and presented with believers
row.note: God raises believers with Jesus and presents them together; resurrection is explicitly a movement into God's presence rather than a terminal vanishing.

row.basis: book of remembrance before God
row.note: A book of remembrance is written before God for those who fear him, closely paralleling the commentary's divine book in which past generations are neither lost nor forgotten.

row.basis: God will not forget
row.note: Even a mother's possible forgetting is contrasted with God's refusal to forget Zion, giving a precise divine answer to human memory's loss.

row.basis: every deed written in a book
row.note: The maxim's seeing eye, hearing ear, and book recording all deeds make the commentary's claim that the Lord neither loses nor forgets a concrete ethical-accounting image.

row.basis: God is not unjust to forget work
row.note: Hebrews explicitly denies that God forgets the readers' work and love, a direct theological counterpart to the commentary's negation of divine loss and forgetting.

row.basis: no sparrow forgotten before God
row.note: Not one of five sparrows is forgotten before God; the small-scale saying gives a vivid instance of divine attention that does not lose what creatures lose from sight.

row.basis: books opened for the dead's judgment
row.note: The dead stand before the throne and are judged from opened books, joining the commentary's book, non-forgetting, and no-one-absent motifs in one judgment scene.

row.basis: no escape through Sheol or heaven
row.note: Even descent to Sheol or ascent to heaven cannot evade God's hand; it is a close prophetic analogue to the claim that none can disappear from the day of reckoning.

row.basis: nothing hidden from God's sight
row.note: No creature is unseen before God and all are exposed to him, supplying the divine-sight side of the commentary's assertion that nobody can be absent from judgment.

row.basis: idols wholly pass away
row.note: In Isaiah's day-of-the-Lord scene idols utterly pass away, closely matching the commentary's judgment image of fabricated objects vanishing from their makers.

row.basis: manufactured gods perish from earth
row.note: The Aramaic denunciation says gods that did not make heaven and earth will perish, a specific biblical counterpart to invented divine partners disappearing at judgment.

row.basis: an idol has no real being
row.note: Paul's claim that an idol has no real existence supplies a Christian conceptual counterpart to the commentary's false, fabricated objects proving absent rather than dependable.

row.basis: from a drop to dust, then account before the King
row.note: The maxim makes a person consider both the destination of the body in dust and the coming account before God; it places earth-bound mortality and divine encounter side by side.

row.basis: God takes and will restore the soul
row.note: The morning prayer says God will take the soul and restore it in the time to come, a liturgical Jewish expression of temporary loss followed by restoration.

row.basis: two ways, of life and death
row.note: The Didache's opening contrast of the Way of Life and the Way of Death makes the commentary's two kinds of going into an early Christian ethical map.

row.basis: Joseph's waterless pit contains snakes and scorpions
row.note: The rabbinic reading of Genesis 37:24 says the pit lacked water but held snakes and scorpions, making the hidden descent more perilous and sharpening the preservation implicit in Joseph's later emergence.

row.basis: return to dust
row.note: Genesis' mortality judgment sends the human back to dust without adding a resurrection in this utterance; the commentary begins with comparable earth-loss but answers sceptical finality with new creation and meeting God.

row.basis: the dead's memory is forgotten
row.note: Qoheleth says the dead's remembrance is forgotten, a bounded human-memory counterpoint that makes the commentary's stronger claim about God's unfailing book and knowledge more pointed.

row.basis: lamp for feet and light for path
row.note: The psalm supplies light specifically for feet and a path, directly reversing the commentary's scene of people unable to see where the road lies.

row.basis: lost sheep sought by its master
row.note: The speaker confesses, "I have gone astray like a lost sheep," and asks to be sought; this turns dalal as unknown departure into a personal petition for recovery.

row.basis: "This is the way; walk in it"
row.note: A voice guides those turning right or left by naming the way they must walk, a particularly close divine answer to the request to be guided on a path.

row.basis: blind groping and failure in one's ways
row.note: The curse imagines groping at noon as a blind person in darkness and not succeeding in one's ways, combining impaired sight with failed direction.

row.basis: upward path of life versus Sheol below
row.note: For the wise, the path of life rises upward in order to turn away from Sheol below; its vertical destinations sharpen the commentary's distinction between a journey that arrives and one that is lost.

row.basis: wandering from understanding to the assembly of the dead
row.note: Proverbs gives wandering from the way of understanding an explicit resting place among the dead, a grave outcome for directionless movement.

row.basis: earth opens its mouth and swallows Korah's company
row.note: The earth literally opens and swallows the rebels and their households, a forceful Torah scene for the commentary's paired images of swallowing and disappearance into ground.

row.basis: earth closes over the living as they descend to Sheol
row.note: The swallowed group goes down alive to Sheol, the earth closes over them, and they perish from the assembly; it gives the earth-loss image its punitive, destinationless extreme.

row.basis: God swallows up death forever
row.note: Isaiah reverses the commentary's swallowing image by making God consume death itself, then remove tears; the shared bodily image serves an opposite eschatological result without claiming cognacy.

row.basis: sea depths made into a way for the redeemed
row.note: God makes a way through the depths of the sea for the redeemed to cross, a vivid counter-image in which water becomes a directed road rather than a place where things disappear.

row.basis: God sees every human way and step
row.note: God's eyes are upon a person's ways and see every step, directly answering the commentary's difference between a traveller leaving human sight and nothing being lost to divine knowledge.

row.basis: waters over the head and the cry "I am cut off"
row.note: The lamenter describes water closing over his head and concludes that he is cut off, a close scriptural scene of disappearance in water.

row.basis: calling God's name from the lowest pit
row.note: From the lowest pit the speaker calls on God by name, making the concealed pit a place from which relationship and appeal remain possible.

row.basis: God comes near to the pit-bound caller
row.note: God draws near when the speaker calls and says not to fear; this supplies the response that turns the preceding pit-disappearance into an encounter rather than abandonment.

row.basis: the King of the world raises the dead
row.note: The martyred brother says that the King of the world will raise those who die for the law to everlasting life, a direct Jewish rebuttal to death as final loss.

row.basis: hearts go astray and do not know God's ways
row.note: Hebrews applies the wilderness generation's persistent going astray to its failure to know God's ways, directly coupling dalal-like error with an unrecognized divine route.

row.basis: exclusion from God's rest
row.note: The divine oath that the straying generation will not enter God's rest supplies the destination denied to those who have not known God's ways.

row.basis: confidence to enter the holy places
row.note: The verse names entry into God's holy presence as the believers' goal, the arrival required to read the next verse's new and living way as more than a road metaphor.

row.basis: new and living way through the veil
row.note: Jesus inaugurates a new and living way through the veil; the Christian image joins a specifically living route to access before God.

row.basis: Red Sea crossed as dry land, Egyptians swallowed by it
row.note: Israel crosses the sea as dry ground while the Egyptians are swallowed when they attempt it, sharply contrasting water as a way of arrival with water as consuming loss.

row.basis: make straight paths for your feet
row.note: The exhortation to make straight paths for the feet seeks restoration rather than dislocation for the lame, a pastoral Christian use of straight-path imagery.

row.basis: God will no longer remember sins
row.note: Hebrews uses divine non-remembrance as covenantal forgiveness of sins, not as failed recall; that deliberate sense of "not remember" usefully distinguishes it from the commentary's claim that God never loses knowledge or forgets.
